advances: The full-selection equality charge holds with the absolute constant \(C=441\), independently of midpoint multiplicity. No restriction to \(A_0<1\) is needed. The proof charges bad center rows directly and obtains a strict aggregate contraction for the remaining center masses.
author: research-agent
proof:
For each \(x\in A\), let \(d_x\) be the number of pairs \(e\in\mathcal P\) with \(j_e=x\), and define \(t_x=Kp_x\) and \(g_x=(2d_x+1)t_x\). Distinct pairs have disjoint endpoint sets, because each occupies a different two-point parity class. Every pair center belongs to \(A\). Every distinct reflected pair about a supported \(x\) is a member of \(\mathcal P\), and the midpoint equality makes each of its two oriented contributions to \(H_p(x)\) equal to \(p_x\). Consequently \(H_p(x)=(2d_x+1)p_x\), so \(g_x=KH_p(x)\). The scalar \(g_x\) is a dimensionless reflected-row sum; it is not an auxiliary center probability.

For every parity \(\eta\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n\), including empty classes, put \(R_\eta=Kr_\eta\). Introduce the dimensionless quantities
$$
F=\sum_{x\in A}t_x(g_x-1)^2,
\qquad G=\sum_\eta(R_\eta-1)^2,
\qquad B=\sum_{x\in A}d_xt_x^2=\sum_{e\in\mathcal P}t_{j_e}^2.
\tag{1}
$$
Since \(\sum_xt_x=\sum_\eta R_\eta=K\) and there are exactly \(K\) parity classes, these definitions give \(F=K\mathcal V\), \(G=K\mathcal D\), and \(B=K\beta\). In particular, \(F,G,B\ge0\). The exact pair equality is \(t_{u_e}t_{v_e}=t_{j_e}^2\), and expansion within the at-most-two-point parity classes gives
$$
\sum_\eta R_\eta^2=\sum_xt_x^2+2B=\sum_xt_xg_x.
$$
It follows that
$$
F+2G=\sum_xt_xg_x^2-K=K\bigl(K^2b(p)-1\bigr).
\tag{2}
$$
This proves the asserted identity for \(\mathcal E\).

Call a nontrivial center \(x\), meaning \(d_x\ge1\), good when \(7/8\le g_x\le9/8\), and bad otherwise. Let \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm g}\) and \(\mathcal J_{\mathrm b}\) be these two sets, and write
$$
B_{\mathrm g}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal J_{\mathrm g}}d_xt_x^2,
\qquad B_{\mathrm b}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal J_{\mathrm b}}d_xt_x^2,
\qquad M_{\mathrm g}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal J_{\mathrm g}}t_x.
$$
Thus \(B=B_{\mathrm g}+B_{\mathrm b}\). For every good center, \(2d_x+1\ge3\), whence \(t_x\le3/8\), and
$$
d_xt_x^2=\frac{t_x(g_x-t_x)}2\le\frac9{16}t_x.
\quad\text{Therefore}\quad
B_{\mathrm g}\le\frac9{16}M_{\mathrm g}.
\tag{3}
$$
For a bad center with \(g_x<7/8\), the inequalities \(g_x\le7/8\) and \(1-g_x\ge1/8\) imply \(g_x/[2(g_x-1)^2]\le28\). For a bad center with \(g_x>9/8\), put \(z=g_x-1>1/8\); then \(g_x/[2(g_x-1)^2]=1/(2z^2)+1/(2z)\le36\). Since \(d_xt_x^2\le t_xg_x/2\), summing these bounds yields
$$
B_{\mathrm b}\le36F.
\tag{4}
$$

We next charge the total good-center mass through its parity classes. In a parity class with \(R_\eta<7/8\), the total mass \(t_x\) of its good centers is at most \(R_\eta\), and
$$
R_\eta\le\frac78\le56(R_\eta-1)^2.
$$
Consequently all such classes contribute at most \(56G\) to \(M_{\mathrm g}\).

Consider a good center \(x\) in a parity class with \(R_\eta\ge7/8\). Its own mass \(t_x\le3/8\) shows that this class cannot be a singleton. It therefore determines one pair \(e\in\mathcal P\), in which \(x\) is an endpoint. Write \(\upsilon=t_x\), let \(\omega\) be the other endpoint's dimensionless mass, and put \(\xi=t_{j_e}\). Then
$$
\upsilon+\omega=R_\eta\ge\frac78,
\qquad \upsilon\le\frac38,
\qquad \omega\ge\frac12>\upsilon,
\qquad \upsilon\omega=\xi^2.
\tag{5}
$$
This parity class contains at most one good center, because two good-center masses would sum to at most \(3/4<7/8\).

If \(j_e\) is good, then \(\xi\le3/8\). By (5),
$$
\omega=\frac{R_\eta+\sqrt{R_\eta^2-4\xi^2}}2
\ge\frac{7+\sqrt{13}}{16}>\frac58.
$$
Hence \(\upsilon=\xi^2/\omega\le(8/5)\xi^2\). If \(j_e\) is bad, the bound \(\omega\ge1/2\) in (5) gives \(\upsilon\le2\xi^2\). These alternatives exhaust the possibilities, because \(j_e\) is the center of the nontrivial pair \(e\).

Distinct high-mass parity classes determine distinct pairs, and each contributes at most one good center. Summing their preceding bounds, and then including the low-mass parity classes already charged to \(G\), gives
$$
M_{\mathrm g}\le\frac85 B_{\mathrm g}+2B_{\mathrm b}+56G.
\tag{6}
$$
All pairs centered at the same atom are already counted with their multiplicity in \(B_{\mathrm g}\) or \(B_{\mathrm b}\). Thus (6) requires no multiplicity bound and remains valid when center and endpoint roles overlap.

Combining (3) and (6) produces the strict aggregate contraction
$$
B_{\mathrm g}
\le\frac9{10}B_{\mathrm g}+\frac98B_{\mathrm b}+\frac{63}2G,
\qquad
B_{\mathrm g}\le\frac{45}4B_{\mathrm b}+315G.
$$
Using (4) and nonnegativity now gives
$$
B=B_{\mathrm g}+B_{\mathrm b}
\le\frac{49}4B_{\mathrm b}+315G
\le441F+315G
\le441(F+2G).
$$
Divide by \(K\) and use (1) to obtain \(\beta\le441\mathcal E\). This proof also covers the empty pair set, empty good-center set, and empty bad-center set, with the same definitions and no divisions by their masses.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(K=2^n\), and let \(A\subset\mathbb Z^n\) be finite and nonempty. Assume every coordinatewise parity class contains at most two points of \(A\), and the midpoint of every distinct same-parity pair in \(A\) belongs to \(A\). Let \(p_x>0\) for every \(x\in A\), with \(\sum_{x\in A}p_x=1\), and extend \(p\) by zero outside \(A\). Let \(\mathcal P\) contain every unordered pair \(e=\lbrace u_e,v_e\rbrace\) of distinct same-parity points in \(A\), and write \(j_e=(u_e+v_e)/2\). Require the exact equality \(p_{j_e}^2=p_{u_e}p_{v_e}\) for every \(e\in\mathcal P\). There is no bound on the number of pairs having the same midpoint.

Use the full reflected sum, including both orientations of each nonzero displacement and the zero displacement once:
$$
\begin{aligned}
H_p(x)&=\sum_{v\in\mathbb Z^n}\sqrt{p_{x+v}p_{x-v}},
&b(p)&=\sum_{x\in A}p_xH_p(x)^2,\\
\beta&=K\sum_{e\in\mathcal P}p_{j_e}^2,
&\mathcal V&=\sum_{x\in A}p_x(KH_p(x)-1)^2,\\
r_\eta&=\sum_{x\in A\cap(\eta+2\mathbb Z^n)}p_x,
&\mathcal D&=K\sum_{\eta\in\lbrace0,1\rbrace^n}r_\eta^2-1,
\qquad \mathcal E=\mathcal V+2\mathcal D.
\end{aligned}
$$
Here \(\mathcal V\) is exactly the target's \(V_{\mathrm{dev}}\), \(\mathcal D\) is its \(D\), and \(\mathcal E\) is its \(E\); \(H_p,b(p),r_\eta,\beta\) retain their stated full-selection meanings and normalizations. Then \(\mathcal E=K^2b(p)-1\) and \(\beta\le441\mathcal E\). Every probability and the entire support remain unchanged. In particular, the conclusion holds whether or not the auxiliary cubic sum \(A_0=K^2\sum_xp_x^3\) is less than one.
